.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 219 PM EDT Sunday...

No significant changes were made to the forecast. We will
continue to monitor conditions Monday afternoon and evening for
the potential for stronger storms and locally heavy rain.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 219 PM EDT Sunday...

1. Drier conditions continue this afternoon through early 
Monday, then showers and thunderstorms return Monday afternoon 
through early Tuesday as a weak front moves across the region. 
Another dry period is likely Tuesday afternoon into Wednesday.

2. Wet end to the week but drier weather expected next weekend.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 219 PM EDT Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A weak cold front has moved to our south and east,
ushering in drier conditions to northern New York and Vermont that
will last into Monday. Aloft, wildfire smoke is flowing into 
the region as well, though it looks like it should stay at high 
elevations and not descend to the surface. Highs today and 
Monday will be warmer than seasonal normals for early to mid 
August, with afternoon temperatures hitting the mid 70s to 80s 
each day. High pressure will be in control tonight, producing 
favorable conditions for radiational fog in the typical valley 
locations, mainly across Vermont, as lows fall into the 50s to 
mid 60s. A warm front is expected to lift through the region 
Monday afternoon, increasing chances of precipitation again into
the 60-90% range for most areas outside the Connecticut River 
Valley. Strong storms are not out of the question Monday 
afternoon as high resolution models indicate around 1000 J/kg 
surface CAPE and 40 knots bulk shear available. The potential 
for severe storms may come down to the timing of frontal 
boundaries in our region aligning or not aligning with best 
instability and shear. Highest instability is expected in 
southern portions of our forecast area, including the central 
Adirondacks, southern Champlain Valley, and southern/south- 
central Vermont. Meanwhile, highest shear is anticipated across 
the Champlain Valley and portions of Vermont in the afternoon, 
resulting in an area of overlap between these two. A surge of 
moisture with precipitable water values 1.50-1.75" could also 
result in heavy downpours in any showers or thunderstorms across
the region. Widespread showers and storms will linger into 
Monday night as another weak cold front moves through and 
temperatures fall into the 50s to mid 60s again. Another dry 
period is likely Tuesday afternoon through Wednesday as drier 
air filters in behind this second cold front. Highs in the 70s 
and lower 80s both Tuesday and Wednesday will be much closer to 
seasonal averages than we've seen of late, and relative humidity
values will also decrease to more comfortable levels toward the
midweek.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Deterministic guidance continues to be in good agreement 
that a strong mid-level shortwave and associated jet streak will 
help to amplify a longwave trough across the Northeast on Thursday 
and Friday. The GFS, ECMWF, and CMC are all in good agreement in the 
general evolution on the longwave pattern but still differ slightly 
on the exact timing when precipitation will return to the North 
Country. The general consensus, supported by the NBM, shows rain 
chances ramping up quickly during the pre-dawn hours on Thursday 
with widespread rainfall expected across the upper level trough 
swings through Thursday afternoon. A seasonably strong cold front 
will push through, likely behind the mid-level trough passage which 
is expected to bring below normal temperatures and drier weather to 
the region for Friday and much of the upcoming weekend. Deep layer 
ridging is expected to develop by Saturday which should bring plenty 
of sunshine with highs in the 70s, light winds, and dewpoints in the 
40s to lower 50s. 

There is also the potential for a few strong to possibly severe 
storms Thursday if we can get out of the "junky" clouds and rain in 
the morning. Models do suggest some strong convergence associated 
with the frontal boundary but the big question will be whether or 
not we can destabilize. Right now, it doesn't look promising for 
stronger storms but the AI and machine learning algorithms are 
giving us around a 10-15 percent chance for at least one report of 
severe weather. It'll be something to watch in the coming days but 
nothing to be concerned about at this time.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z SUNDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Through 18Z Monday...VFR conditions will continue through the
TAF periods for most sites with the exception of KMPV and KEFK
where periods of MVFR, IFR, and VLIFR fog are expected overnight
tonight. Given the trends from this morning, it likely won't be
until 13Z that fog is finally able to mix out with VFR
conditions returning at these sites thereafter. Winds will be
gusty at times out of the west with gusts likely no higher than
20 knots with winds going calm/light and variable overnight.
Winds will shift to the south after daybreak tomorrow with some
10-15 knots winds possible through the day on Monday.

Outlook...

Monday Night: VFR. Chance SHRA, Chance TSRA.
Tuesday: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Tuesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday: VFR. Chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Wednesday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Chance
SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Thursday: VFR/MVFR conditions possible. Likely SHRA, Chance TSRA.
Thursday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Slight
chance SHRA.
Friday: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.

&&

VT...None.
NY...None.
